blocks.text: Allergies result from hypersensitivity of the immune system to weak antigens that cause no response in most people. The substances that cause them, allergens, include dust, moulds, pollen, cat dander, certain foods and some medicines such as penicillin.

After exposure to an allergen some people make E-antibodies, which bind to mast cells, usually found in connective tissue around blood vessels. The mast cells release histamine, which starts the inflammatory response: blood vessels dilate, fluid leaks out, and sneezing, runny nose and itching follow. In some people histamine causes life-threatening anaphylactic shock, in which swelling makes breathing difficult.

blocks.alt: A single row: an allergen binds a B-cell, which becomes a plasma cell releasing E-antibodies; the E-antibodies attach by their stems to a mast cell; when the allergen binds them, the mast cell releases histamines, which cause symptoms.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.16: Events of allergic response (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.16).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Allergen, B-cell, E-antibodies, Plasma cell, Mast cell, Histamines, Symptoms.

blocks.text: Antihistamine drugs block histamine and give temporary relief. Many allergies are also treated by injecting extracts of the allergen, desensitization, which makes the body produce G-antibodies in the blood; when the allergen enters it is destroyed by G-antibodies before it meets the E-antibodies.
Autoimmune diseases result when the immune system cannot distinguish the body's own cells from foreign material, so it attacks and destroys the body's cells and tissues.

blocks.text: Most medicines for autoimmune diseases suppress immunity in general.

T and B cells normally attack only foreign molecules and cells, because each person's cells carry self-proteins, a molecular 'fingerprint' that the person's own T and B cells recognise. After an organ transplant the donated organ's self-proteins may not match the recipient's, so the recipient's T cells may attack its cells and B cells make antibodies against its proteins: transplant rejection.

items: Doctors look for a donor whose self-proteins match the recipient's as closely as possible.
Drugs suppress the recipient's immune response to the organ, but they also reduce the ability to fight infections.
Monoclonal antibodies can be used to destroy the T cells that attack the transplant.
Stem cells can be used to make a new immune system that recognises the transplant as self.

blocks.title: Matching donors
blocks.text: Identical twins have a 100% self-protein match, and the best matches occur within a family. The order of preference is identical twin, then sibling, then parent, then unrelated donor; the chance of an unrelated donor matching the recipient is 1 in 100,000-200,000.
